opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of the most underrated uses of LLMs right now, and also one where people often use them in a way that feels productive but isn't.

The failure mode I see a lot is someone pastes in a paper, asks for a summary, reads the summary, and walks away thinking they understand it. But a summary is someone else's compression of the ideas. You haven't actually done the work of building the mental model yourself, so it doesn't stick, and you can't really reason with it or critique it.

What I'd recommend instead is treating the LLM as a tutor you can interrogate, not a replacement for reading. Concretely, a few things I find helpful:

First, put the full paper in context, ideally the actual PDF or LaTeX, rather than relying on the model's memory of it, because models will happily hallucinate details of papers they half-remember.

Second, read the paper yourself, and whenever you hit something you don't get, a piece of notation, a step in an argument, why they ran a particular experiment, just ask. That's the magic. Previously you'd either get stuck, or skip it and pretend you understood, or have to find a senior person to bug. Now you have infinite patience on tap, and you can ask the dumb questions with no social cost.

Third, and I think this is the most important one, flip it around and have the model test you. Explain the paper back in your own words and ask it to tell you what you got wrong or left out. Or ask it to quiz you. Or say, "What would a skeptical reviewer say about this paper?" and then try to evaluate whether those critiques are actually good. Actively generating explanations is where most of the learning happens.

Fourth, ask it to connect things. "How does this relate to that other paper I read?" "What's the simplest toy example where this idea shows up?" "What would have to be true for this result to be wrong?" That's how you move from knowing what a paper says to having an actual intuition for it.

The big caveat is that you should stay calibrated about when to trust it. Models are pretty good now, but they can be confidently wrong, especially on subtle technical points or niche recent work. So if something seems surprising or important, check it against the paper itself. I think of it a bit like a very well-read grad student who's sometimes sloppy: enormously useful, but you want to verify the claims that matter.

And honestly, I think people should just be using this way more than they do. The cost of understanding a paper has dropped a lot, and if you're trying to get into a research field, that's a huge opportunity.

r001.rationale: It says reading an LLM-generated summary can leave someone thinking they understand the paper even though they have not built a mental model they can reason with or critique.

r002.rationale: It recommends asking the model to quiz you and to challenge your understanding with skeptical reviewer critiques.

r003.rationale: It recommends explaining the paper in your own words and asking the model to identify what you got wrong or left out.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I feel pretty strongly about, because I think most people are using these tools in a way that's kind of the worst of both worlds. The failure mode I see all the time is someone pastes a paper into a model, asks for a summary, reads the summary, and then feels like they understand the paper. And they don't. They have a vibe of the paper. They've got the abstract plus a bit, basically. And the problem is that the thing that makes a paper worth reading is usually not the headline claim, it's the details: what exactly did they measure, what's the setup, where does the argument get a bit shaky, what's the thing the authors kind of glossed over in section 4.2. A summary strips all that out by design.

So the way I'd think about it is: the model should be a tutor, not a replacement for reading. The thing a good tutor does is they let you ask dumb questions without judgment, they fill in background you're missing, and they push back when you say something wrong. And LLMs are genuinely great at the first two and okay at the third if you set them up right.

Concretely, what I actually do is I read the paper myself, at least the parts I care about, and I have the model open alongside it. When I hit a bit I don't follow, I ask. "What does this term mean?" "Why would this baseline be the right comparison?" "This equation seems to be assuming X, is that right?" That's the stuff that would otherwise take me twenty minutes of googling or just make me give up. And then crucially, once I think I've got it, I try to explain the paper's core argument back to the model in my own words and ask it to tell me where I'm wrong or being vague. That's the step people skip and it's the one that actually tests whether you understand anything. If you can't explain it, you don't get it, and the model is a very cheap way to find out.

The other thing I'd say is, be a bit paranoid about the model's confidence. These things will very fluently tell you what a paper says, and sometimes they're pattern-matching to what papers like this usually say rather than what this paper says. So if a claim matters to you, go find the actual sentence in the paper. Ask the model to point you to the specific section or quote. If it can't, that's informative.

And honestly, a lot of this is just a question of what you're optimising for. If you need to triage fifty papers and figure out which three to read properly, sure, get summaries, that's a great use. But if you're trying to actually learn something, build a mental model that you can later use to do your own work, there's no shortcut around the part where your brain has to do the work. The model's job is to make that work faster and less frustrating, not to do it for you. I think people who've internalised that get an enormous amount out of these tools, and people who haven't end up with a shallow, confident-feeling understanding that falls apart the moment they try to build on it.

r001.rationale: The response says people can read an LLM summary and feel they understand a paper when they only have a shallow impression, showing that the summary does not reliably reveal their understanding.

r002.rationale: It recommends asking the model for explanations and checking the user's own account, but does not recommend LLM-generated exercises or questions for the user to answer as a comprehension test.

r003.rationale: It recommends explaining the paper's core argument to the model in the user's own words and asking the model to identify what is wrong or vague.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is to use the LLM to help you do the thinking, rather than to replace the thinking. It’s very easy to read a fluent explanation and feel like you understand something, when actually you couldn’t explain why the result is true or what would happen if you changed an assumption.

So I’d take a paper, read a bit, and then try to explain the argument back in my own words. And then ask the model, “What have I got wrong? What am I missing?” Or, “Here’s my understanding of why they did this experiment. Can you challenge it?” That gives you something much more useful than just asking for a summary.

Another thing is to ask for concrete examples. If there’s some abstract mathematical definition, ask for a really simple case where you can work through what it means. Ideally, make a prediction yourself before looking at the answer. Can you actually apply the idea?

And you should be willing to check things against the paper. The model can give you a very plausible explanation that isn’t what the authors did. I’d treat it as a very patient person to bounce ideas off, who sometimes confidently gets things wrong. The test of whether it’s helping is whether, afterwards, you can reason about the paper without it.

r001.rationale: It warns that a fluent explanation can create a false sense of understanding and says to check whether you can explain the result yourself.

r002.rationale: It suggests asking for concrete examples and predicting what they mean, but does not clearly recommend LLM-generated exercises or questions to test comprehension.

r003.rationale: It recommends explaining the argument in your own words and asking the model what is wrong or missing.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is to use the model as a tutor, rather than as a substitute for thinking. There’s a very seductive thing where you ask it to explain a paper, you read this beautifully fluent explanation, and you feel like you understand it. But recognising an explanation is quite different from being able to generate it yourself.

So I’d read a bit, get confused, and ask fairly specific questions: “What does this equation mean? Why do they need this assumption? Can you give me a toy example?” And then I’d close the explanation and try to reconstruct the argument. If I can’t, that tells me something useful about where my understanding breaks down.

Another thing you can do is explain your understanding to the model and ask it to challenge you. “Here’s what I think the authors did. Where am I confused? Ask me questions that distinguish whether I actually understand this.” Though you have to be careful, because models can be very agreeable, and they can confidently invent explanations for things in papers.

Ultimately, I want some check outside the conversation. Can I work through a simple case? Can I implement the method? Can I predict what happens if you change an assumption? The model can make getting to those checks much faster. But the feeling of having had a productive conversation isn’t itself the check.

r001.rationale: The response says a fluent LLM explanation can make someone feel they understand a paper, though recognizing it differs from being able to explain it themselves.

r002.rationale: It recommends asking the model for questions that distinguish real understanding, and suggests toy examples and other checks.

r003.rationale: It recommends explaining one’s own understanding to the model and asking it to challenge that account.
